text: Artificial intelligence is a transformative force that drives and accelerates the evolution of learning and learning sciences. AI revolutionises teaching and learning with the potential to enhance efficiency, personalization, and accessibility. Advanced real-time personal assistants transform learning and learning models, and translation tools boost global collaboration, making learning truly inclusive and boundary free. AI-assisted virtual learning environments provide new ways to experience and learn in the virtual or augmented world. We continuously evolve our programs and learning environments to meet the increasingly diverse needs of future students and trainees – towards a model where learning can happen anywhere, anytime, and with anyone. Education is a lifelong journey, thriving on adaptability and bold ideas. Lifelong learning opens new perspectives and increases flexibility in both personal and technological development. Rapid technological advances, globalisation, and evolving job markets demand continuous upskilling and reskilling. Nations benefit from and increasingly require an adaptable workforce, making lifelong learning crucial for economic growth. Demographics necessitate ongoing education throughout careers and [ORGANISATION] democratises access to education by offering programs for learners of all ages. By embracing curiosity, collaboration, and responsibility, we create lasting impact throughout careers. Our diverse information and training programs empower people at every stage of life – whether seasoned professionals exploring new horizons, children uncovering the wonders of science and engineering, or citizens engaging with our research – while we, in turn, benefit from this exchange and channel it into our institutional growth. We are the lifelong partner for the educational needs of our students and alumni. Attracting the brightest minds worldwide is our unwavering goal and we are committed to taking the steps needed. We cultivate an environment where exceptional talent unfolds – supported, challenged, and inspired at every stage, independent of their background. We are committed to all employees at [ORGANISATION], offering them exciting and attractive career and development opportunities.

As the major national centres of higher education, universities have a particular role in graduate education. As the largest and highest ranked research university in the country, [ORGANISATION] has a pre-eminent place in this regard. The number and achievements of our masters and doctoral graduates have a significant bearing on the University’s reputation and ranking, and on our contribution to society. Since holders of postgraduate degrees occupy many influential roles in the public and private sectors, postgraduate degree completions are important measures of the University’s wider social and economic impact. Our success in recruiting postgraduate students should thus be matched by significant improvement in the rate at which students complete postgraduate degrees.

Key actions: • Enhance processes for training supervisors and allocating students to them so as to maximise the quality of supervision and probability of student success. • Provide students with clear expectations as to the scope and duration of their studies. • Support research postgraduate students (e.g. via scholarships and research resources) to ensure that they complete their programmes within the allotted time.

Our reputation with students, their parents and families, and our communities rests significantly on the quality of our teaching and learning. We expect our graduates to be independent and critical thinkers, open to new ideas, possessing intellectual curiosity and integrity, and to have a mastery of a body of knowledge and professional skills. They should be able to use information discerningly, to show tolerance and an understanding of diverse value systems and views, and to have the potential and the wish to contribute in a leadership role to national and global intellectual, social, scientific, economic and cultural development.

Failure as Method Why this matters. The research traditions [ORGANISATION] stewards have always carried failure as a productive element of inquiry: the failed experiment that reframes the question, the rejected draft that prompts the eventual argument, the discarded composition that the artist returns to as the work matures. The institutional cultures around this knowledge have weakened across the sector over recent decades, partly under pressure from publication metrics that reward only the converged result. The Plan rebuilds them, at the institutional rather than the individual scale.

What we’ll do. 1. The University will establish the Centre for Failure Studies, anchored across the Research School of Social Sciences and the [ORGANISATION], with cross-appointments held jointly with the [ORGANISATION] & [PLACE]. 2. The University will convene the annual [ORGANISATION] Failure Conference, at which researchers from across the four colleges present primary accounts of inquiries —8—

that did not produce the anticipated result, with the inaugural conference scheduled for 2027. 3. The University will establish the Public Errata register at [ORGANISATION] Press, in which corrections, retractions, and methodological updates to [ORGANISATION]-affiliated published work are aggregated, classified, and indexed at institutional rather than perjournal level. 4. A “Methodological Failure” elective stream will be developed and made available to every honours and HDR program offered by the University, as a sequenced curriculum on the productive uses of failure across the disciplines. How we’ll know. • One hundred per cent of [ORGANISATION]-affiliated peer-reviewed publications submitted from 2028 will carry a methodological appendix declaring at least one substantive false start, with no exception sustained for more than a single review cycle. • The Public Errata register will receive at least two hundred submissions per year from 2029, sustained at that level through 2031.

Vision By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be a national university recognised — within the country, in its region, and across the global research community — as an institution that speaks in its own voice and means what it says. The University will have demonstrated, over the run of this Plan, that a serious national institution can take its own register seriously without sliding into parody, and that the country is the better served for the demonstration. The disciplines will have been tended with care; the partnerships will have been held in fair exchange; the federal capital will be a more recognisable seat of national scholarship in 2031 than it was in 2026.

Strategic pillars Fair Dinkum National Capability Context. The University was established to serve the country in the most direct sense. Establish a National Voice Audit, published annually, examining the University’s external-facing strategic literature for register, voice, and clarity, with audit findings reported to Council. 2. Convene the Sovereign Capability Forum twice yearly, bringing the country’s policy community, the academy, and senior public service together around a small set of long-horizon questions of national capability. 3. Establish a Fair Dinkum Research Programme: a published list of research initiatives the University considers central to the country’s sovereign capability, with funding committed across the plan period and protected against ordinary funding-cycle reallocation. —9—

The day-to-day work of delivery sits with the executive, supported by the standing committees of Council and the academic and professional communities of the university. This plan is the university’s commitment to its community and to the country. Its implementation is our shared responsibility.

Establishing and leveraging interdisciplinary research initiatives We will establish a core set of interdisciplinary research initiatives that we want to be known for – hubs of innovation that unite experts across diverse fields to tackle complex local and global challenges. These initiatives will take different forms, including pan-university and virtual models, enabling flexibility and collaboration at scale. Each initiative will be grounded in challenge-based themes such as smart manufacturing, AI, advanced materials, regional resilience, health sciences and environmental sustainability, with a focus on delivering meaningful impact for society and our communities. We recognise that ethical and inclusive solutions to society’s most pressing challenges happen at the intersection between science and technology, and the humanities, arts and social sciences. Understanding people and how we relate, communicate and connect is fundamental to building a better future in an increasingly digital and complex world. It is through collaboration across disciplines, perspectives and communities, that we will unlock the most groundbreaking solutions – we are better together.

Our interdisciplinary research initiatives will deliver innovative solutions to issues such as climate change, renewable energy, circular economies, water security and sustainable development. Our researchers will work across disciplines and sectors to translate knowledge into tangible outcomes, shaping more resilient environments, industries and communities. We will play a vital role in addressing the UN [[ORGANISATION]] and contribute to critical national priorities, such as [PLACE]’s energy transition, by accelerating impactful research and innovation. In doing so, we will contribute to strengthening [PLACE]’s productivity through more sustainable and future-focused industries.

Our agenda Institutional Assurance and Foresight Why this matters The University has, in effect, run four plans at once for as long as it has had four kinds of unit reporting on their own progress in their own terms and on their own schedule. That approach served the institution reasonably well when its scale was smaller and its obligations to funders and government were lighter; it no longer does. Institutional Assurance and Foresight exists to give the University a single, continuously current account of how its strategic commitments — across every pillar, including this one — are actually tracking, and to direct attention and resourcing toward whichever commitment needs it most in a given quarter, rather than waiting for the commitment to fail publicly first. That redirection is itself now a standing feature of how the University is run, not a one-off correction — a scale of change that, we recognise, asks more of every pillar lead than any previous planning cycle has. External advice on how such a system should be built, and how it should be received by the people it measures, is drawn from the University’s own research capability: Dr [PERSON], Senior Research Fellow in the [ORGANISATION], whose fieldwork traces how planning is actually practised inside institutions, will advise the program on how delivery-confidence scoring lands with the units it covers, and on where the architecture’s design should bend to fit the practice rather than the reverse.

What we’ll do 1. Establish an AI-governance early-warning system spanning every pillar and budget line of this plan, reporting a live delivery-confidence score to the Council and the Executive. 2. Bring each pillar’s reporting into a single assurance architecture, replacing the separate reporting rhythms each pillar has historically kept. 3. Direct a standing share of pillar funding, reallocated quarterly, toward whichever pillar’s delivery-confidence score is lowest in that quarter — including, where the data supports it, this pillar’s own build-out.

text: [PLACE] the Trajectory Early Why this matters. A commitment made without evidence of the trajectory it backs is a commitment the University discovers the shape of only after making it — in the first year of an appointment, the first term of an enrolment, the first cycle of a partnership. [PLACE] the trajectory early moves that discovery to before the offer is drafted, where it is still cheap to be wrong. The appointing panel or admissions committee that reads the trajectory late is not being careless; it is simply working with the only evidence the process gave it, gathered after the decision it was meant to inform. What we’ll do. 1. Every advertised continuing and fixed-term academic and professional role will require a trajectory portfolio — a structured account of the candidate’s likely next five years, evidenced against commitments the candidate has previously made and kept — alongside the standard application, reviewed by the appointing panel before an offer is drafted. 2. Every Higher Degree by Research and coursework admission will carry a trajectory statement at the point of offer, held by the enrolling school and revisited at the candidate’s first formal milestone. 3. The [ORGANISATION] will publish a common portfolio template and scoring rubric, adopted by every appointment panel and admissions committee by the end of 2027, with no locally authored alternative permitted to persist past a single review cycle. 4. Application systems will present the trajectory portfolio and the standard application as a single combined submission from 2028, so a candidate completes one process rather than two. How we’ll know. • 100% of continuing and fixed-term academic appointments will draw on a completed trajectory portfolio before an offer is extended, from 2027 onward, with no waiver sustained for more than a single recruitment cycle. • Portfolio review turnaround will hold at fewer than 15 business days from submission to panel recommendation, reported each term. • By 2029, every admissions committee across both Schools will use the common rubric, retiring locally authored alternatives entirely. • Candidate-reported completion time for the combined submission will be published each admissions cycle from 2028, alongside the completion rate.

Vice-Chancellor’s introduction This is the [ORGANISATION]’s strategic plan for the period 2026 to 2031. It sets out the directions the University will pursue over the next phase of its institutional life, and the choices we have made in setting them. The plan reflects our continuing commitment to research excellence, to the depth and seriousness of our educational programs, and to the partnerships through which a national university actually meets the country it serves. It also reflects the recognition that the work of a university is undertaken on a long horizon — shaped by problems we have only begun to see clearly, and by futures whose outlines remain to be drawn.

The directions in this plan have been informed by extensive consultation with our staff, students, alumni, partners, and Council. They are deliberate. They reflect choices made carefully, and they will require sustained effort to deliver. I want to thank the many members of our community who contributed to this plan, and in particular the staff, students, and external partners who pressed us to be both more honest and more ambitious. The result is, I believe, a plan worthy of the university we are working to become. I commend it to the [ORGANISATION] community. The work that follows is ours to do together. Vice-Chancellor and President

Inspired by global leaders in Co-op education and tailored to [PLACE]’s needs, our model integrates work and study without extending time to graduation. Learners gain valuable experience while earning their qualifications, accelerating career outcomes and improving graduate salaries.

In our Higher Degrees by Research (HDR) programs, this includes co-designing, co-supervising and co-funding projects with industry partners, alongside opportunities for PhD candidates to undertake research internships. We’re committed to remaining among the top universities in [PLACE] for employability and starting salary. By enabling placements alongside study, we’ll ensure graduates are ready to work from day one – with many learners transitioning directly into roles with their placement hosts. Through paid placements we’ll further breakdown financial barriers – boosting equity, access and making education and real-world experience more accessible to a diverse range of learners.

By 2040, we aim to have thousands of active partners across diverse sectors – co-designing curriculum, hosting learners, upskilling staff and co-investing in facilities like our campus-based technology parks. These partnerships will create a strong pipeline of talent research, innovation and opportunity, with employers turning to [PLACE] as their university of choice. Co-op will shape how we deliver education, research and support services. It will become a whole-of-university ethos – guiding every decision and driving strategic transformation.

Foreword from the Vice-Chancellor [PERSON] Plan articulates the direction of the [ORGANISATION] across the period 2026 to 2031. The Plan is framed, throughout, by the institutional legacy of [PERSON], the University’s most consequential alumnus, whose centenary falls in the final year of the plan period. It is not the working group’s view, and it is not Council’s view, that institutional planning should reach unduly into the past. The view that has emerged across consultation, however, is that the [PERSON] tradition — often referred to in the University’s older literature simply as “the [PERSON] disposition” — continues to distinguish [ORGANISATION] from the institutions with which it is most often compared, and that the centenary year provides a structural occasion for the University to take fresh form around the disposition rather than merely commemorate its founder.

The disposition is well documented. [PERSON] characterised it, variously, as “the patient examination of the half-baked”, “the work of taking the unbaked seriously”, and, in the often-cited formulation from the 1948 notebook, “the discipline of recognising what is, in fact, packaged for use”. It produced, across the productive period of the 1920s and 1930s, the inventions for which he remains best known — the wooden magnet, the boxed spark plug sparks, the bottled spirit-level bubbles, the dehydrated water pills, the clockwork motor vehicle, and the around-the-corner hammer, among others — and it shaped the institutional culture of the University in ways that have continued, with admirable consistency, across the eight decades since. The Plan accordingly addresses the [PERSON] tradition as a substantive institutional commitment. It does so across four priorities — the [PERSON] legacy itself, the [PERSON] research method, the education of the [PERSON] posterity, and the stewardship of the [PERSON] Collections, Archives, and Spirit — each unpacked in the body of this document. We commend the Plan to the University community in the conviction that an institution which knows its tradition is an institution better placed to do its tradition’s continuing work. Vice-Chancellor and President

The view that has emerged across consultation, however, is that the [PERSON] tradition — often referred to in the University’s older literature simply as “the [PERSON] disposition” — continues to distinguish [ORGANISATION] from the institutions with which it is most often compared, and that the centenary year provides a structural occasion for the University to take fresh form around the disposition rather than merely commemorate its founder.

The disposition is well documented. [PERSON] characterised it, variously, as “the patient examination of the half-baked”, “the work of taking the unbaked seriously”, and, in the often-cited formulation from the 1948 notebook, “the discipline of recognising what is, in fact, packaged for use”. It produced, across the productive period of the 1920s and 1930s, the inventions for which he remains best known — the wooden magnet, the boxed spark plug sparks, the bottled spirit-level bubbles, the dehydrated water pills, the clockwork motor vehicle, and the around-the-corner hammer, among others — and it shaped the institutional culture of the University in ways that have continued, with admirable consistency, across the eight decades since. The Plan accordingly addresses the [PERSON] tradition as a substantive institutional commitment. It does so across four priorities — the [PERSON] legacy itself, the [PERSON] research method, the education of the [PERSON] posterity, and the stewardship of the [PERSON] Collections, Archives, and Spirit — each unpacked in the body of this document. We commend the Plan to the University community in the conviction that an institution which knows its tradition is an institution better placed to do its tradition’s continuing work. The Plan treats integration as a substantive institutional discipline. Microdose. A sub-perceptual dose; in the Plan, a low-intensity, regularly administered formation-oriented seminar distributed across the long arc of a degree. Set. The mindset, intention, and preparation with which the University approaches a given inquiry. The first of the two classical terms the Plan invokes. Setting. The physical, relational, and temporal conditions in which inquiry is conducted. The second of the two classical terms the Plan invokes. Sub-perceptual dose. A dose at a level below the threshold of immediate perception but sufficient, when regularly administered, to produce durable formation. In the Plan, the term denotes the principle underlying the Microdose Curriculum.

Looking ahead The decade ahead will ask of universities a different kind of attention from the one the sector has spent the previous forty years cultivating: the willingness to take seriously the conditions under which inquiry produces durable understanding, rather than the willingness to multiply the inquiries themselves. The work is patient and largely invisible from outside. Much of it is the slow work of preparation, of holding, and of integration that no audience ever sees directly. But the conditions on which a national research university’s contribution to the country depends are not built in any other way. The medicine, properly held, integrates. [ORGANISATION] will continue the work of holding it.

A Community of Calibrated Feel Why this matters. Attunement is a capability of people, and it is only an institutional capability when the people who hold it are many, aligned, and renewed. A felt sense that lives in a handful of senior practitioners is a dependency, not an assurance arrangement. The third priority therefore builds the community: accredited practitioners across every school and portfolio, a shared sensibility maintained through deliberate calibration, and a pipeline through which the feel is passed on faster than it retires. What we’ll do. 1. Develop and deliver Foundations of Vibe Literacy, an accredited program through which every continuing staff member acquires the shared vocabulary, calibration practices, and recording conventions of structured attunement. 2. Establish a practitioner accreditation pathway, from foundation through panel ready to senior practitioner, with progression assessed — appropriately — by attunement, and with senior accreditation renewed through participation in calibration convenings. 3. Build calibration into the institutional rhythm, through regular cross-school convenings in which practitioners re-align their reads against shared cases, drawing on the [ORGANISATION] line where an intensive format serves the cohort. 4. Recruit and promote for feel, incorporating demonstrated attunement capability into academic and professional promotion criteria and into selection for institutional leadership roles. This is the environment this plan answers. Not a single new pressure, but the accumulation of many small ones, each asking the University to be more certain, earlier, and for longer, about the trajectories it is prepared to back. [ORGANISATION]’s setting sharpens the point rather than softening it. A university that draws its staff, students, and partners from across a single region carries a longer institutional memory of the commitments it has made there than a larger, more transient institution might; a trajectory backed badly is not easily forgotten by the people around it. Place, in that sense, is not a backdrop to this plan but a discipline on it — the University answers, over the decade ahead, to the same community it commits to, and a commitment that does not hold up under evidence will be noticed close to home before it is noticed anywhere else.

Where we are headed By 2031, no commitment [ORGANISATION] makes will outlive the evidence that justified it. This is a narrower ambition than it first sounds, and a more demanding one. It does not mean the University will commit to less, or more slowly. It means that whatever the University commits to — an appointment, an admitted cohort, a partnership, a continuing career — will carry a live account of the trajectory behind it, refreshed on a published schedule rather than assumed to still hold. A university that can show, at any point across the life of a commitment, the evidence that still justifies it, is a university whose confidence in its own decisions can be checked rather than simply taken on faith. That is the institution this plan builds toward. Reaching it means treating evidence of trajectory as infrastructure rather than paperwork: something built once, resourced properly, and maintained on a schedule the University publishes and keeps to, in the same way it maintains any other system its people and partners rely on.

Capability Through Clear Custodianship Why this matters Shared research equipment and actively maintained datasets currently rely on inherited knowledge of who looks after what, passed on informally when a custodian moves between labs or leaves the University altogether. Formal, attested custodianship protects research capability directly: an instrument that is calibrated on schedule and handed on cleanly serves every project that depends on it, not just the one that happened to be running when it was last checked. The University’s research strategy already depends, in practice, on this kind of custody working quietly in the background; this priority simply makes that dependency visible, named, and reviewable rather than trusting it to survive the next round of staff turnover by luck.

1. Assign a named custodian to every item of shared research equipment and every actively maintained dataset, published on the research-infrastructure register alongside the Stewardship Register. 2. Require an annual custodianship attestation, renewed or formally reassigned, with a documented succession protocol triggered the moment a custodian departs. 3. Route every custodian-reported fault directly into the relevant lab’s maintenance queue, closing the loop between a report and its resolution. 4. Publish a lightweight custodianship handbook for each equipment category — calibration cadence, fault-reporting steps, succession checklist — so a new custodian inherits a procedure, not just a name. How we’ll know • 100% of shared research equipment carries an active, attested custodian by 2029. • Average custodian tenure at handover exceeds eighteen months, with a documented successor named within a fortnight of any departure. • Equipment fault-to-resolution time falls year-on-year for the remainder of the plan. • Every equipment category carries a published handbook, reviewed at each custodianship handover without exception.

Education That Shapes the Future Why this matters. The graduates who pass through [ORGANISATION] during the plan period will work for forty to fifty years across fields whose shape we cannot fully predict. The strongest preparation we can offer is not a fixed body of knowledge — though knowledge matters — but the dispositions and forms of practice that allow a person to keep learning, keep contributing, and keep adapting through long working lives in unsettled fields. Education at [ORGANISATION] should equip graduates to do that work well. What we’ll do. 1. Renew the undergraduate curriculum around durable capabilities and forms of practice, including studio-style and ensemble learning formats in which students rehearse the moves of inquiry and collaboration alongside academic content, rather than acquiring content in isolation from the work it is meant to support. 2. Deepen the integration of research into education at every level, so that students at every stage encounter live questions, contribute to ongoing work, and develop the judgement that comes from sustained engagement with real problems. 3. Strengthen postgraduate and professional education as a coherent program of study, including renewed Masters offerings, expanded micro-credentialing in areas of national capability need, and professional pathways that complement the HDR program rather than competing with it. Roadmap The plan will be delivered in four overlapping phases across the period to 2031. The phases are sequential in emphasis but not in start — each priority will have activity under way from the first year of the plan.

Foundation (2026) In the first year, we will put in place the governance, baselines, and foundational investments needed to deliver the plan. Each priority will have a designated executive sponsor, a dedicated implementation team, and a published baseline against which progress will be measured. Foundational investments — in flagship research programs, in educational redesign, and in the digital and physical infrastructure that supports them — will commence.

Acceleration (2027-2028) Through 2027 and 2028, the major investments and program changes set out in this plan will reach scale. New postgraduate programs will commence; flagship research initiatives will reach operational maturity; the campus precinct refresh will deliver its most visible early outcomes. Consolidation (2029-2030) Through 2029 and 2030, the focus will shift from build to sustained operational delivery. Vice-Chancellor’s introduction This Strategic Plan articulates the direction of the [ORGANISATION] across the period 2026 to 2031. The Plan does so through a framing the working group settled on early in the drafting process and held throughout: that an institution of [ORGANISATION]’s complexity is best understood as a production — a long-running production with an overture, character arcs, ensemble numbers, and a closing standing ovation that the institution intends to earn rather than expect. The framing is not metaphorical decoration. A long-running production has the same operational characteristics as a long-running national institution. It requires a script that the company believes in. It requires rehearsal time that the schedule must protect. It requires a producer’s discipline about which numbers are working and which are not. And it requires an honest assessment, at the end of each season, of where the production is on its run.

This Plan describes how the University will run its production over the next five years. It describes the kinds of standing-ovation moments — the showstoppers, the eleven o’clock numbers, the encores — that the institution intends to earn, and it describes the kinds of supporting work, often invisible from the stalls, that those moments require. We commend the Plan to the University community in the conviction that a national university which understands its own staging is a national university more likely to do its work well. Vice-Chancellor and President

A plan written for a turbulent decade has to do something a stable plan does not: it has to take the next contribution seriously, whatever shape it arrives in, and it has to keep building on what is working rather than quietly setting it aside. The directions that follow have been chosen with that disposition in mind.

The plan reflects extensive consultation with our staff, students, alumni, and partners over the course of 2025, and structured deliberation by Council and the executive across the same period. The directions it sets out are deliberate. They will require sustained effort, candid review, and a willingness to revise where evidence requires it. I commend this plan to the [ORGANISATION] community. The work that follows is ours to do together, and I am confident in the contribution that [ORGANISATION] will continue to make to [PLACE], the region, and the world over the period ahead. This plan describes how we will sustain and renew that purpose over the period to 2031. Four strategic priorities organise the work of the plan period. Each is developed in detail in the body of this document, with a premise, a set of transformation initiatives, success measures, and an indicative phasing for delivery.

These priorities are interdependent. None can be fully realised in isolation, and the plan is best read as a description of the university we are working to become over the period ahead: ambitious about what universities are for, honest about the work required, and recognisably [ORGANISATION].

Advanced physical and digital infrastructures play an increasingly important role in both research and education. UiO will work systematically to achieve more sharing and better accessibility to infrastructure and data resources. There is a great need for long-term investments, and a roadmap has been drawn up for priorities. Based on the roadmap, UiO will invest in, develop and maintain infrastructure that helps to strengthen our international position as a research-intensive university.

It's important to be successful in the competition for talent. UiO will conduct goal-oriented recruitment and develop outstanding researchers and research environments. The process of recruitment and assessment shall be open and transparent with an emphasis on quality and academic assessments. Younger researchers should be offered predictable frameworks for the development of their careers.

A positive and strong research culture based on high scientific standards and ideals must form the premise for all research activities. Knowledge and awareness of research ethical norms is something all academic environments and all levels of the organisation must safeguard through systematic training and continuous awareness.

The social challenges of our times require global solutions, and UiO will renew its international educational cooperation. Through strengthened [PLACE] cooperation, UiO will reach out globally in new ways and with a greater collective power than today. Together with other research-intensive universities, UiO will facilitate integrated courses of study across languages, national borders and subjects.

Based on a stronger link between research and education, UiO will continue to develop as an ambitious educational institution. Professional and general education shall be more closely linked to research activities and working life and motivate students to increase their efforts and achievements. In order to meet students' social involvement, academic desires and ambitions, the study options should be made more flexible, and there should be an increase in the number of interdisciplinary study options. UiO will become a hub for student innovation in the [PLACE] region.

The University’s own experience over the current planning period bears this out. Work already published from within our schools has found that a system recolouring a shared kitchenette’s compost-bin lids changed remarkably little about what actually went into them, and that a fault-reporting instrument installed to replace a handwritten log measured its own uptime more confidently than it measured the thing it was installed to track. These are not failures of any single instrument. They are what happens when a great deal of institutional attention goes into measuring and anticipating, and comparatively little goes into the plainer question of who is holding the thing steady in between. This plan sets out to close that gap directly, deliberately, and by name.

Our ambition By 2031, every asset, process, and shared resource the University holds will carry a single named, accountable steward, published on a register anyone in the University community can check. That ambition is deliberately narrower than “improve accountability” and deliberately broader than any one School’s remit. It asks nothing exotic of the University — only that the habit already practised in its most visible instruments, the [ORGANISATION]’s named convenor, the [ORGANISATION]’s named custodians, extend all the way down to the smallest shared thing the University holds. Priority 4: A Capable and Durable Institution None of the above is possible without renewed institutional foundations. Over the plan period we will invest in the digital, physical, and human infrastructure on which [ORGANISATION] depends, and we will work toward an institutional culture in which every member of the community can do their best work.

Our position A university is, in the end, an apparatus for sustaining intellectual work over decades. The settings of that apparatus — the buildings, the systems, the cultures of the people who make it run — have to be tended deliberately if the work is to continue.

• Refresh the campus precinct as a working environment fit for the next twenty-five years, with sustained investment in heritage assets, contemporary teaching spaces, and student amenities. • Build a culturally safe and structurally equitable working environment for all members of the [ORGANISATION] community, with clear measures of progress on representation, retention, and career advancement for staff and students from historically marginalised backgrounds.

Foundational investments — in digital infrastructure, in flagship research initiatives, and in educational redesign — will commence.

Deepen (2027-2028) Through 2027 and 2028, the major investments and program changes set out in this plan will reach scale. New postgraduate programs will commence; flagship research initiatives will reach operational maturity; the campus precinct refresh will deliver its most visible early outcomes. The mid-period review will be undertaken in late 2028.

Ahead-of-Its-Time Research and the [PERSON] Method Premise. The research character of the University has, since [PERSON], been distinguished by a willingness to undertake work whose immediate application is unclear and whose ultimate value depends on the patient unfolding of what later commentators have called the [PERSON] Method: the discipline of taking the halfbaked idea seriously, examining it in its half-baked state, and following it through the patient sequence of testing, recasting, and packaging by which [PERSON] produced, among other things, the wooden magnet, the boxed spark plug sparks, and the celebrated dehydrated water pills. The Plan extends the Method into a structured contemporary research posture.

Initiatives. 1. Establish the [PERSON] Method Fellowship: a ten-year research fellowship scheme for early-career researchers prepared to commit to work whose applications are unlikely to be visible within the term of the fellowship, with a published carrying capacity for the scheme set at two cohorts at any one time. 2. Convene the Wooden Magnet Working Group, named for one of [PERSON]’s signature investigations, charged with identifying research directions the University considers fifty years ahead of their time and protecting them against the funding cycle’s ordinary impatience. 3. Maintain and expand the [PERSON] Collections held at the Menzies Library, including the original sketches, working papers, and surviving prototypes, with the collection made progressively available for direct consultation by researchers across the [PLACE] region. Measures. 1. By 2031, the [PERSON] Method Fellowship will be funding two active cohorts, with the first ten-year cycle settled and an open call for the next. 2. The Wooden Magnet Working Group will have met quarterly from 2026 onwards, with minutes published in full. 3. By 2028, the [PERSON] Collections will have been fully digitised and made publicly accessible, with a published cataloguing standard shared with comparable national archives.

True to our roots as an ancient [PLACE] university, our degree programmes combine breadth and depth, and draw their strength from the quality of our research. Writing as Engineered Practice Context. Writing at the University — student, scholarly, professional, administrative — is increasingly co-produced with technical systems whose contribution is rarely articulated. [ORGANISATION] will treat the writing apparatus of the institution as scholarship, not infrastructure, and will articulate it for use by the University community and for the broader sector.

Commitments. 1. The University will stand up the Centre for Composition Studies, anchored in the School of Literature, Languages and Linguistics with cross-appointments held jointly across the School of Computing and the [ORGANISATION] & [PLACE]. 2. A “Writing Apparatus” elective stream will be developed and made available to every undergraduate degree program, with a minimum of three sequenced units offered each semester from 2028. 3. The University will establish the [ORGANISATION] Editorial Stack: an institution-wide articulation of accepted, declared, and prohibited writing tools by use class, published openly and revised at twelve-month intervals. Indicators. • One hundred per cent of taught course work at 2000 level and above will publish a “writing apparatus” disclosure to students alongside the standard course outline by 2029. • Three peer-reviewed monographs per year will be published through [ORGANISATION] Press in the Composition Studies series by 2029, sustained through the remainder of the plan period. • An annual [ORGANISATION] Composition Prize, awarded in three categories (drafting, revision, machine-assisted composition), each with a published methodological declaration as a condition of submission.

Visual Composition in Hybrid Media Context. The visual artefacts produced by the institution — figures, diagrams, posters, slides, video, generative output, exhibition materials — pass through compounding technical stacks whose contribution to the eventual artefact is generally invisible to the reader or viewer. [ORGANISATION] will own the visual stack as a site of scholarship and craft.

Our Research Throughout the centuries, researchers at the [ORGANISATION] have generated new insights in medicine, science and engineering, law, social sciences, arts and humanities. Our work has earned many honours and awards, and has contributed to five Nobel prizes. Like our education, our research will be intellectually rigorous. Whether working within our established areas of excellence, or developing interdisciplinary approaches that generate new methods of inquiry, we will tackle theoretical and practical problems. We will generate new knowledge and will connect and combine ideas, addressing economic and societal issues with ambition and imagination.

Our research will be globally excellent and locally relevant. To ensure this, we will engage with our external partners as we plan for the future, and will work collaboratively with them both on and off campus. Our research will be open to all. We will work to share our findings, and to promote open access to academic resources for anyone who wishes to learn. Our research will have impact on our world, and will inform our curriculum, shaping what and how we teach. We will train and support the next generation of researchers, equipping them with the skills they need to develop their expertise and to engage with the challenges of the future.

In these pages, we set out 20 commitments across these four themes. We will address five great challenges of our age. As the digital revolution brings new opportunities, and the climate emergency threatens us all, we commit to delivering outstanding education and research that will shape the lives of our students, and tackle the pressing problems of our world.

Executive summary This plan commits [ORGANISATION] to a single working principle across the decade ahead: no commitment — to a person, a cohort, or a partner — is made, or continued, without evidence of the trajectory that justifies it. Four strategic pillars carry that principle from the moment an offer is drafted through to the moment a portfolio of evidence is finally retired.

Together, these pillars close a gap the University has lived with for longer than it has been comfortable admitting: that a trajectory, once backed, was rarely checked again. The decade ahead will see deepening pressure on natural systems and intensifying transitions across the energy, industrial, and social systems on which our communities depend. Universities are central to navigating these transitions — both through research and through the leadership they educate.

A distinctive position [ORGANISATION] sits in a particular place. We are [PLACE]’s national university, established by an Act of [PLACE] [ORGANISATION] with a charter to serve the nation. We are located in the country’s capital, deeply integrated with the institutions of national life. We are research-intensive at a scale and depth unmatched in the country. And we are home to research and teaching strengths — across the sciences, humanities, social sciences, and policy domains — that are genuinely globally distinctive. This position confers both opportunity and obligation. The opportunity is to make a contribution to the national effort that no other institution can. The obligation is to do so with the seriousness, the independence, and the strategic clarity that the country deserves from its national university. This plan describes how we will meet that obligation over the years to 2031.

This vision is ambitious and focused. It reflects our distinctive mission, our particular institutional strengths, and the moment in which we find ourselves. It is grounded in eight decades of demonstrated capacity and oriented toward the next.
